title: Encode and Decode Strings — design encode/decode for list of strings.
shortTitle: Encode and Decode Strings — Length-Prefixed Serialization

s1_definition.profdef: Encode and Decode Strings designs a reversible scheme to serialize a list of arbitrary strings into one string and parse it back exactly, even when the strings contain any character including the delimiter. The robust scheme is length-prefixing: each string is written as its length, a separator, then the raw string content, so decoding reads a length, then reads exactly that many characters, with no character being special. It runs in linear time over the total content.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India must pack several free-text transaction remarks into a single line to send over a wire and then unpack them perfectly on the other side. A naive packer glues remarks with a comma, but a remark itself might contain a comma and break everything. The reliable packer writes, before each remark, how many characters it has, like "12#Rent payment", so the reader always knows exactly how far to read, no matter what characters the remark contains.
s1_definition.oneliner: Prefix each string with its length and a separator, so decoding reads exactly that many characters and no character is ever ambiguous.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Encode and Decode Strings designs a reversible scheme to serialize a list of arbitrary strings into one string and parse it back exactly, even when the strings contain any character including the delimiter. The robust scheme is length-prefixing: each string is written as its length, a separator, then the raw string content, so decoding reads a length, then reads exactly that many characters, with no character being special. It runs in linear time over the total content.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India must pack several free-text transaction remarks into a single line to send over a wire and then unpack them perfectly on the other side. A naive packer glues remarks with a comma, but a remark itself might contain a comma and break everything. The reliable packer writes, before each remark, how many characters it has, like "12#Rent payment", so the reader always knows exactly how far to read, no matter what characters the remark contains.

**One line to remember:** Prefix each string with its length and a separator, so decoding reads exactly that many characters and no character is ever ambiguous.

sections.s2_technical:
The tempting approach is to join the strings with a delimiter such as a comma or a newline and split on it when decoding. This fails whenever any input string contains that delimiter, because the split produces the wrong pieces. Escaping the delimiter can patch it but is error-prone and bloats the output. The clean, delimiter-safe scheme is length-prefixing, sometimes called chunked encoding.

For encoding, you process each string in order. You compute its length, write that length as digits, write a non-numeric separator such as a hash character, and then write the raw string content exactly as-is. You concatenate these chunks for all strings. The crucial property is that the string content is never scanned for special characters, so no character is dangerous and no escaping is needed.

For decoding, you keep a read cursor at the start. You read digits until you hit the separator, which gives you the length as a number. You skip the separator, then read exactly that many characters as the next string, regardless of what those characters are, including hashes, commas, or newlines. You advance the cursor past those characters and repeat until the whole encoded string is consumed. Because the length told you precisely how far to read, the content is reconstructed byte-for-byte.

A senior point is why the separator being between the length and the content is unambiguous even though content can contain the separator. When decoding you only ever interpret characters as the length while you are in the digit-reading phase, which stops at the first separator. Once you switch to reading content by count, you never look for a separator, so a separator inside the content is just data. The number tells you exactly when content ends, so you re-enter the digit phase only at the right boundary.

Another senior point is empty strings and Unicode. An empty string encodes as length zero followed by the separator and no content, which decodes correctly because you read zero characters. For Unicode, you should define length in terms of a consistent unit, either characters or bytes, and encode and decode with the same unit and charset, typically UTF-8 byte length, so multi-byte characters survive. In banking, remarks may contain names in regional scripts, so I standardize on UTF-8.

A small finance-domain example: encoding `["Rent", "EMI,HDFC"]` yields `"4#Rent8#EMI,HDFC"`, and decoding reads `4`, then four characters `Rent`, then `8`, then eight characters `EMI,HDFC`, recovering both exactly despite the embedded comma.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India batches several free-text transaction remarks for Rajesh and Priya into a single payload to transmit between services, and the receiving service must reconstruct the exact list, even though a remark might contain commas, hashes, or newlines. A naive delimiter join corrupts such remarks. Designing a length-prefixed encode and decode is exactly this.

This is exactly how Encode and Decode Strings works in Java — writing each string's length and a separator before its raw content so decoding reads exactly that many characters.

Problem 2 — Some remarks are empty and some contain the separator character itself, and both must round-trip perfectly, and remarks may contain regional-script names requiring consistent charset handling. This shows the empty-string case, the delimiter-safety property, and Unicode care.

What the code will do: a `RemarkCodec` with `encode(List<String> remarks)` and `decode(String payload)` using length-prefixing with a hash separator. The demo round-trips a list of remarks including awkward characters.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the demo
java -cp target/classes com.bank.remarkcodec.RemarkCodecDemo
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the remarks are `Rent`, `EMI,HDFC`, `fee#2`, and an empty string.

Step 1 (encode): `Rent` has length four, so we write `4#Rent`. `EMI,HDFC` has length eight, so we write `8#EMI,HDFC`, and notice the comma inside is written as plain content with no special treatment.

Step 2 (encode): `fee#2` has length five, so we write `5#fee#2`, and notice the hash inside the content is written as plain data even though hash is our separator. The empty string has length zero, so we write `0#` with no content. The full payload is `4#Rent8#EMI,HDFC5#fee#20#`.

Step 3 (decode): the cursor starts at zero. We read digits until the first hash, getting `4`, skip the hash, and read exactly four characters `Rent`. The cursor advances past `Rent`.

Step 4 (decode): we read digits until the next hash, getting `8`, skip the hash, and read exactly eight characters `EMI,HDFC`, so the embedded comma comes back correctly because we read by count, not by searching for a comma.

Step 5 (decode): we read `5`, skip the hash, and read exactly five characters `fee#2`, so the embedded hash is recovered as content because once we are reading by count we never look for the separator. Finally we read `0`, skip the hash, and read zero characters, recovering the empty string. The decoded list exactly equals the original.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T19:30:00Z INFO Encoded payload = 4#Rent8#EMI,HDFC5#fee#20#
2026-10-26T19:30:00Z INFO Decoded 4 remarks
2026-10-26T19:30:00Z INFO Round-trip equal = true
2026-10-26T19:30:00Z INFO Recovered = [Rent, EMI,HDFC, fee#2, ]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  encode(["Rent","EMI,HDFC","fee#2",""])
    │ write len + '#' + raw content (content never escaped)
    ▼
  payload = "4#Rent8#EMI,HDFC5#fee#20#"
    │
    ▼  (over the wire)
    │
    ▼
  decode(payload): read digits→len; skip '#'; read exactly len chars
    │ 4→"Rent"  8→"EMI,HDFC"  5→"fee#2"  0→""
    ▼
  ["Rent","EMI,HDFC","fee#2",""]  (exact round-trip)
    ▼
  Output: reconstructed remark list
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Remark Codec ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Length-prefixed (chunked) serialization: delimiter-safe      │
  │  Codec pair: encode/decode are exact inverses                 │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: codec only serializes/deserializes string lists           │
  │  O: swap separator or charset without changing callers        │
  │  D: callers depend on encode/decode contract, not the format  │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              RemarkCodec              │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────── │
  │  - SEP: char = '#'                     │
  │  + encode(remarks): String             │  O(total chars)
  │  + decode(payload): List<String>       │  O(total chars)
  └───────────────────────────────────────┘
      decode contract:
        Pre:  payload produced by encode (len#content repeated)
        Post: exact original list, any chars including SEP
        Read by count after SEP; never search content for SEP

  ── State Diagram: Decode Cursor ──────────────────────────

  [i<len] ──read digits to '#' → L──→ [read exactly L chars → add]
      │ i>=len                                │
      ▼                                       └→ i = start + L
  [DONE: list]

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────

  1. RemarkCodecDemo.main()
  2.   → encode(remarks) → "4#Rent8#EMI,HDFC5#fee#20#"
  3.   → decode(payload)
  4.     → read len, skip '#', read len chars, repeat
  5.     → return exact original list
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Encode and Decode Strings is about designing a reversible scheme to pack a list of arbitrary strings into one string and parse it back exactly, even when the strings contain any character. The naive join-on-a-delimiter approach breaks the moment an input contains that delimiter, so I use length-prefixing: before each string I write its length, a separator such as a hash, and then the raw content untouched. The content is never scanned for special characters, so no character is ever dangerous and no escaping is needed.

Decoding mirrors that exactly. I read digits until the separator to get the length, skip the separator, and then read exactly that many characters as the next string, whatever those characters are, then advance and repeat. The number tells me precisely where the content ends, so a separator or comma or newline inside the content is just data, never a boundary, because once I switch to reading by count I never search for the separator again.

The nuances I call out are empty strings and Unicode. An empty string encodes as length zero and the separator with no content, which decodes by reading zero characters. For Unicode I define the length consistently, typically as the UTF-8 byte length, and use the same charset on both sides, so multi-byte regional-script characters survive the round trip. In a bank those remarks often contain names in regional scripts, so this matters.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to batch free-text transaction remarks for Rajesh and Priya into a single payload transmitted between services and reconstruct the exact list on the other side, even when a remark contained commas or the separator character itself. Explaining why length-prefixing is delimiter-safe, how decoding reads by count, and the empty-string and charset handling shows the interviewer that I think about correctness for all inputs, not just the easy ones.
